card.stem: A fixed frame triple-glazed wooden window is fitted in the external wall of a dwelling house, as shown. The external wall is a 450 mm concrete block wall with a full-fill insulated cavity. The wall is plastered on both sides. The bottom of the concrete cill is located 400 mm above finished floor level. The ground floor is an insulated suspended timber floor with 25 mm tongue-and-groove hardwood flooring. The wooden joists are 200 mm × 40 mm.
card.questionText: To a scale of 1:5, draw a vertical section through the ground floor and window. Show the typical construction details from the bottom of the strip foundation, through the suspended timber floor and the external wall to a level 200 mm above the bottom frame of the window. Include three typical dimensions on your drawing.

rows.contextNote: Best three details, 4 each (3 for drawing, 1 for annotation). Typical sizes in the scheme’s model: R.C. strip foundation 1350 × 450 mm; 100 mm block leaves; 250 mm full-fill cavity with basalt-coated low-conductivity ties; 19 mm external render; 15 mm internal plaster.

Best five details, 4 each (3 for drawing, 1 for annotation). Marking menu: compacted hardcore and sand blinding; radon barrier; R.C. concrete subfloor; dwarf walls; wallplate and DPC; ventilation pipe/cover/sealed; floor joists at 400 mm centres; airtight membrane and floor insulation; airtight membrane and tape to the floor perimeter; T + G flooring; skirting. Typical sizes: 150 mm subfloor; 100 mm dwarf walls; 100 × 75 mm wallplate; 200 × 40 mm joists; 200 mm floor insulation; 25 mm T + G flooring; Ø100 mm ventilation pipe.

Best three details, 4 each (3 for drawing, 1 for annotation). Marking menu: concrete window cill; DPC wrapped around the cill; thermally broken window frame; window board; triple glazing; airtight tapes at the cill; vertical DPC.
Three typical dimensions shown on the drawing, 1 each.

card.questionText:
Calculate the U-value of the floor, given the construction has the following sequence and data: Ceramic tile thickness 12 mm; concrete floor slab thickness 150 mm; floor insulation thickness 50 mm; radon barrier thickness 0.25 mm; sand blinding thickness 50 mm; hardcore thickness 175 mm; subsoil thickness 300 mm.
Thermal data of the ground floor: resistance of internal top surface of floor (R) 0.104 m2 ⁰C/W; resistivity of ceramic tiles (r) 0.770 m ⁰C/W; conductivity of concrete floor slab (k) 1.180 W/m ⁰C; conductivity of floor insulation (k) 0.022 W/m ⁰C; conductivity of radon barrier (k) 0.250 W/m ⁰C; conductivity of sand blinding (k) 0.160 W/m ⁰C; conductivity of hardcore (k) 1.350 W/m ⁰C; conductivity of subsoil (k) 1.600 W/m ⁰C.

rows.verbatim: Internal surface resistance Ceramic tile Concrete floor slab Floor insulation Radon barrier Sand blinding Hardcore Subsoil
rows.contextNote: Eight resistances, 3 each, by R = T/k (or R = T × r for the tiles): internal surface 0.104 (given); ceramic tiles 0.012 × 0.770 = 0.009; concrete floor slab 0.150/1.180 = 0.127; floor insulation 0.050/0.022 = 2.273; radon barrier 0.00025/0.250 = 0.001; sand blinding 0.050/0.160 = 0.313; hardcore 0.175/1.350 = 0.130; subsoil 0.300/1.600 = 0.188. All in m²°C/W.
Total resistance Rt = 3.145 m²°C/W (the sum of all the resistances).
U = 1 ÷ Rt = 1 ÷ 3.145 = 0.318 W/m²°C, with units.

card.stem: Careful design detailing is required to prevent the penetration of dampness into a dwelling house. card.questionText:
(a) Discuss two reasons why it is important to ensure that moisture does not penetrate into a house.

(b) Using notes and freehand sketches, show best practice design detailing that will prevent the penetration of moisture at any two locations circled on the drawing.

(c) Describe, using notes and freehand sketches, two different materials that are used to prevent the penetration of moisture into the house at the locations circled.

rows.contextNote: Point 4 and discussion 4. Such as: health, mould growth on internal walls harming the occupants; structural stability, timber roof members rotting over time; thermal comfort, damp insulation between the joists working less well.

A second, different reason. Such as: appearance, with mould, discoloured walls, bubbling paint and rusting metal; the cost of replacing wooden doors, windows or flooring that swell and warp; higher energy bills, as damp air takes more energy to heat or cool.

rows.verbatim: Preventing moisture penetration at two locations
rows.contextNote: Any two of the three circled locations, each note 4 and sketch 10 = 14. Back of chimney: a lead back gutter welted over a tilting fillet and under the breather membrane; the breather membrane or roofing felt carried under the back gutter and lapped up the chimney; a lead cover flashing overhanging the gutter. Front of chimney: the breather membrane carried under the battens and taped to the chimney; a lead front apron flashing dressed on top of the slates and covered by the lead above; the lead carried 150 mm above the lowest point where the stack leaves the roof. Head of Window: a stepped DPC so moisture does not reach the inner wall; the window frame sealed with mastic so wind-driven rain cannot reach the internal leaf.

Note 4 and sketch 4. Such as: lead, malleable, durable and resistant to corrosion, used for flashings, valleys and gutters; a damp proof course (DPC), impervious, flexible, lightweight and embossed to bond with the mortar.

A second, different material: note 4 and sketch 4. Such as: a breather membrane or roofing felt, water-resistant but vapour-permeable, fixed under battens outside the insulation; slate (natural or fibre cement), nailed to battens through two holes and shedding water to the gutter.

card.stem: “The energy used in heating, lighting and in supplying power to a dwelling needs to be reduced, but the energy required to build it also must be addressed. This is the so-called embodied energy, the energy required to dig raw materials out of the ground and transport them to a factory where they are turned into metals or plastics. This embodied energy can account for up to 50% of the total energy consumed during the life of a low-energy-use home. It can be reduced substantially by using natural materials.” Adapted from: The Green Self-Build Book – how to design and build your own eco-home – by Jon Broome. Published by: Green Books Ltd. ISBN: 978 1 903998 73 1
card.questionText: Discuss the above statement in detail.

rows.verbatim: Discussion: Point 1 (4 for point, 6 for discussion)
rows.contextNote: Point 4 and discussion 6. Such as: locally sourced materials cut transport and so embodied energy; imported granite and imported timber carry high embodied energy, while timber grown in Ireland is low in embodied energy and carbon neutral.

rows.verbatim: Discussion: Point 2 (4 for point, 6 for discussion)
rows.contextNote: Point 4 and discussion 6. Such as: cement manufacture produces 900 kg of CO2 and SO2 for every 1000 kg of cement, so using less concrete, or cement made with GGBFS (40% less embodied energy), cuts embodied energy; durable native timbers such as cedar, larch and Douglas fir need little processing.

rows.verbatim: Discussion: Point 3 (4 for point, 6 for discussion)
rows.contextNote: Point 4 and discussion 6. Such as: smaller floor areas and narrow single-room plans spanned by standard timber, with no structural steel; low-embodied-energy insulation such as recycled fibreglass, cellulose or local hemp; hempcrete; stone driveways in place of concrete. Three distinct, well-argued points are needed.
